title: The $94 Excursion
voice: female, ~50, plus-size narrator, friendly Midwestern, wry and warm, a little self-deprecating, conversational pace

caption: I almost threw away a $94 cruise excursion because I knew my feet wouldn't make it. Three pairs of $165 to $180 sneakers had already let me down. Then a woman who walks in a body like mine told me what I'd been getting wrong.
headline: The Shoe That Got Me Up the Ruins
script:
Ninety-four dollars. That's what I was ready to throw away on a cruise excursion I already knew I couldn't finish.

The Mayan ruins at Costa Maya. Two miles of gravel paths and old stone steps in ninety-degree heat.

My sister had paid for hers in March. I had a whole speech ready about a stomach bug.

Let me back up.

I'm Denise. I'm fifty-one, I do medical billing from a desk in Toledo, and I wear a size twenty-two. I'd never been on a cruise in my life.

My sister Carla booked it for my birthday. Seven nights, four ports, an excursion at every stop. She was so excited I couldn't tell her I was scared.

Not of the ocean. Of my feet.

So I did what everybody says. I bought good sneakers.

Hokas first. A hundred and sixty-five dollars. They felt amazing on the store carpet.

I wore them to the outlet mall for a practice run. Four hours in, a sharp stabbing pain in the bottom of my heel.

Then Brooks, a hundred and forty. Then On Clouds, a hundred and eighty, because my coworker swore by hers.

Same story every time. Fine at breakfast. By midafternoon, they felt like they'd shrunk two sizes.

Rock bottom was the county fair, three weeks before we sailed. Two hours in, I was on a hay bale holding everybody's lemonade while Carla and the kids walked the barns without me.

That night I iced both feet and opened the cruise app to cancel the ruins.

Here's what stopped me.

Carla's friend Rhonda came over to help us pack. Rhonda's a big girl like me, and she takes three cruises a year. She's climbed those ruins twice.

She looked at my three shoe boxes and said, "Honey, stop taking shoe advice from people who don't walk in your body."

Then she explained it the way nobody ever had.

A port day is about twenty thousand steps. Every one is your whole weight landing on two feet. When you carry more, every step lands harder.

Those fancy running shoes are more foam than support. That's why they feel so good in the store.

But foam packs flat. Once it's flat, your arch drops and your heel takes every hit. That's the stabbing.

And feet swell in the heat. So the shoe that fit at breakfast is too tight by lunch.

She said, "Most of us blame our weight. But the shoe is the part you can change."

So that's what I looked for. An arch built into the shoe, not a pad that flattens. An upper that stretches.

Room for my toes. And real grip, because ship decks get wet.

Rhonda pulled up the ones she wears. The Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe from Comfort Wear.

About sixty dollars. I almost laughed, after paying a hundred and eighty for the last pair.

The arch support is built into the shoe, so there's nothing to pack down or give out. The stretch-knit upper gives as your feet swell.

Wide toe box. Slip-resistant sole.

Honestly, the first two days I kept waiting for the catch. They felt firmer than the Hokas.

Then I did the outlet mall again. Six hours. I drove home and realized I'd never once looked for a bench.

My feet didn't hurt less. They didn't hurt.

Cozumel, cobblestones all morning. Fine.

Nassau, the long walk back to the pier. Fine.

The pool deck at night was slick, and I never slid once.

Then Costa Maya. Two miles of gravel. Stone steps in the heat.

My feet swelled the way they always do, and that knit just gave.

Carla took a picture of me at the top of those ruins. I'm sweaty, I'm red, and I'm grinning like a fool.

It's on my fridge now. Right next to the receipt for that ninety-four-dollar excursion.

Those foam sneakers were never built to carry a body like mine all day. The Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe from Comfort Wear was.

headline: Seventeen Hours. Didn't Miss the Dance.
script:
At my cousin's wedding last fall, I listened to the Cupid Shuffle from the back seat of my car. Barefoot. Door open.

My niece Kayla came out to the parking lot in her party dress. She leaned in the door and said, "Aunt Trish. You promised."

Her own wedding was eight months away. I've promised her that dance since she was six years old.

Let me back up.

I'm Trish. I'm forty-six, I run the front desk at a dental office outside Macon, Georgia, and I've been a plus-size woman my whole adult life.

Kayla is my sister's girl, but I helped raise her. She wanted me with her the whole wedding day.

Hair at seven in the morning. A barn venue with a gravel lot. Pasture photos, then a reception until midnight.

Seventeen hours on my feet.

For my cousin's wedding, I'd bought Hokas. A hundred and sixty-five dollars. Nobody sees your shoes under a long dress, so I might as well be comfortable.

They felt wonderful at the store. By the reception, I had a sharp stabbing pain in my heel, and they felt two sizes too small.

After that, Brooks, a hundred and forty. Then On Clouds, a hundred and eighty.

Same thing every time. Fine in the morning. Done by suppertime.

Rock bottom was Kayla's bridal shower. I stood three hours serving punch, then sat in my car again before I could drive home.

I thought, I'm going to miss her dance. Not because I don't want it. Because my body won't let me.

Here's what changed.

At the final walk-through, the venue coordinator caught me rubbing my heel. Miss Pearl is a big woman in her sixties. She works a hundred weddings a year on that gravel.

She looked at my On Clouds and said, "Baby, stop taking shoe advice from people who don't walk in your body."

Then she sat down and explained it.

Every step, your whole weight lands on two feet. When you carry more, every one lands harder.

Those fancy sneakers are more foam than support. That's why they feel so good when you try them on.

But foam packs flat. Once it does, your arch drops and your heel takes the hit. That's the stabbing.

And by afternoon your feet swell. So the shoe that fit at hair and makeup is pinching by the cake cutting.

She said, "Most of us blame our weight. But the shoe is the part you can change."

So I made a list. Arch support built into the shoe, not a soft pad. An upper that stretches when I swell.

Room for my toes. Grip for gravel and a slick dance floor.

Pearl showed me what she wears. The Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe from Comfort Wear. About sixty dollars.

I'd spent a hundred and eighty on the last pair. I felt a little silly.

The arch is built into the shoe, so there's nothing to pack down or give out. The stretch-knit upper gives as your feet swell.

Wide toe box. Slip-resistant sole.

The first week, honestly, they felt firmer than I expected. I kept waiting for my heel to start.

It never did. I wore them through a long Saturday of errands, then the rehearsal dinner. Nothing.

Not hurt less. Didn't hurt.

Then the wedding.

Hair at seven. I hauled chairs across that gravel. I stood through forty minutes of pasture photos in June heat.

My feet swelled, and the knit just gave.

At ten thirty, the DJ played the Cupid Shuffle.

Kayla found me across the floor, grabbed my hand, and said, "You promised."

I didn't go near my car once that night.

Those foam sneakers were never built to hold me up for seventeen hours. The Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe from Comfort Wear was.

headline: Three Days on Concrete. Front Row.
script:
My daughter played in a volleyball championship last spring. I watched it on a livestream. From a chair in the lobby, two hundred feet from her court.

She got the final kill. Then I watched her look up into the stands for me.

I wasn't there. And I never told her why.

Let me back up.

I'm Marisol. I'm thirty-nine, I'm a bank teller, I have three kids, and I'm a size twenty-four. My middle girl, Ava, is fourteen and plays club volleyball.

Club volleyball means tournaments. Three days in a convention center. Forty courts laid on concrete with thin carpet over it.

Seven in the morning until nine at night. Matches at opposite ends of the building. Then back again.

The other team moms told me to get good running shoes. So I did.

Brooks first, a hundred and forty dollars. Then Hokas, a hundred and sixty-five. Then On Clouds, a hundred and eighty.

They all felt amazing in the store. Every single pair.

And every pair did the same thing. Fine Friday morning. By Saturday afternoon, sharp stabbing pain in my heel, and the shoes felt two sizes too small.

Rock bottom was that spring tournament. By Sunday I couldn't make the walk to the far courts.

My husband carried the cooler. I sat in the lobby with the bags.

That night I soaked my feet in the hotel bathtub with ice from the machine. I cried where nobody could hear.

Here's what changed.

At the next tournament, a grandma from our team named Gloria sat down next to me. Gloria's a big woman like me. She walks every court, every day, all weekend.

She saw me rubbing my heel and said, "Mija, stop taking shoe advice from people who don't walk in your body."

Then she explained it.

A tournament day is close to twenty thousand steps. Every one is your whole weight landing on two feet. When you carry more, every step lands harder.

And concrete doesn't give at all. So the shoe is the only thing between you and the floor.

Those fancy running shoes are more foam than support. That's why they feel so good in the store.

But foam packs flat. Once it's flat, your arch drops and your heel takes every hit. That's the stabbing.

Then your feet swell. The shoe that fit at the first serve is squeezing you by lunch.

She said, "Most of us blame our weight. But the shoe is the part you can change."

So I knew what to look for. An arch built into the shoe, not foam that flattens. An upper that stretches.

Room for my toes. Grip for those slick floors.

Gloria pulled up her pair right there on the bleachers. The Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe from Comfort Wear.

About sixty dollars. The hundred-and-eighty-dollar pair was sitting in my closet.

The arch support is built into the shoe, so there's nothing to pack down or give out. The stretch-knit upper gives as your feet swell.

Wide toe box. Slip-resistant sole.

Honestly, the first week they felt firmer than I was used to. I wasn't sure.

Then I stood at my teller window all week in them. Friday came, and my heel was quiet.

Not hurt less. Didn't hurt.

The fall qualifier was three days. Same convention center, same concrete.

Friday, fine. Saturday, I walked the far courts twice and carried the cooler myself. Sunday, my feet swelled like always, and the knit just gave.

Ava's team made the final again.

I was in the front row. On my feet the whole match.

When it ended, she looked up into the stands. This time she found me on the first try.

I still haven't told her about that lobby. I don't need to.

Those foam sneakers were never built to carry me across that concrete. The Ortho Stretch Cushion Shoe from Comfort Wear was.
